item.text: I’ll check current first party documentation for both tokenizers and make the comparison concrete with cited example counts.

There isn’t a fixed number of extra tokens: it depends on the exact wording and the tokenizer version. A useful rough estimate is that Korean often takes **about 1.5–2× as many tokens** as an English translation. That means roughly **50–100% more** tokens—not a guaranteed rate for every passage.

| Tokenizer | Practical estimate | Source |
|---|---:|---|
| OpenAI | About 1.5–2× the English count for Korean text, as a rough estimate | OpenAI’s [tokenizer](https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer) shows how text is split; its [tiktoken guide](https://github.com/openai/tiktoken) explains that token counts depend on the encoding. |
| Claude | About 1.5–2× as a rough estimate; the ratio varies by text | Anthropic’s [token-counting documentation](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/token-counting) describes counting with Claude’s tokenizer. |

For example, if an English passage uses 1,000 tokens, the estimate would be around **1,500–2,000 tokens** for a Korean translation. For a dependable number, compare the *same meaning* in both languages using the specific model’s tokenizer or token-counting tool; translations can differ in length, and OpenAI and Claude tokenizers can split the same Korean text differently.
